competencies.label: Knowledge, belief and justification
competencies.description: I can explain the difference, with an example.

competencies.label: Arguments and validity
competencies.description: I can identify premises and distinguish validity from truth.

competencies.label: Conditional probability
competencies.description: I can distinguish P(A|B) from P(B|A).

competencies.label: Theories of knowledge
competencies.description: I am comfortable with Gettier cases and justification.

competencies.label: Evidence from other people
competencies.description: I can explain how testimony can support a belief.

03/validity-and-soundness.why: Identify premises and conclusions before testing whether the conclusion follows.

03/formal-fallacies.why: The distinction between validity and truth makes formal errors easier to diagnose.

09/bayes-theorem.why: Conditional probability supplies the notation and ideas used in Bayes’ theorem.

09/common-errors-in-probabilistic-reason.why: Use conditional probability to see why reversing a conditional can mislead.

09/calibration-and-scoring-rules.why: A probability expresses confidence; calibration compares that confidence with outcomes.

05/the-gettier-problem.why: Gettier cases challenge the justified-true-belief account introduced here.

06/foundationalism.why: Clarify what justification asks of a belief before comparing its structures.

06/coherentism.why: Clarify what justification asks of a belief before comparing its structures.

08/the-closure-argument.why: The skeptical argument concerns whether ordinary claims qualify as knowledge.

12/experts-and-novices.why: Expert advice is a special case of learning from another person’s testimony.

12/trust-and-epistemic-dependence.why: Start with testimony before asking when dependence on others is justified.

topics.label: Arguments & disagreement
topics.question: Where does the discussion usually get stuck?

focuses.label: I want to test whether an argument works

steps.why: Separate a conclusion that follows from premises that are actually true.
Turn an everyday claim into an argument you can examine.
Avoid treating a bad argument as proof that its conclusion is false.
Put the distinctions to work on the claim you started with.
Examine recurring mistakes in the form of an inference.
Look for hidden assumptions in persuasive arguments.

focuses.label: We keep talking past each other

steps.why: Find out whether the dispute concerns facts, meanings or values.
Check whether the same word is doing different jobs.
Locate the belief that would actually change the discussion.
Consider when another person’s disagreement is evidence.
Keep inquiry possible when disagreement persists.
Balance receptiveness with standards for evidence.

topics.label: Probability & decisions
topics.question: What would you like to do with uncertainty?

focuses.label: Update my confidence when evidence arrives

steps.why: Learn how prior confidence and new evidence combine.
Check base rates and reversed conditionals before trusting an intuitive answer.
Test whether your confidence matches your track record.
Connect probability judgments with forecasting practice.
Explore what probabilistic updating means for rational belief.
Ask how confidence relates to outright belief.

focuses.label: Understand a statistic or research result

steps.why: Distinguish statistical significance from the claims it cannot establish.
Check whether an association warrants a causal conclusion.
Consider how much weight to put on a single result.
Identify probability mistakes in how the result is presented.
Consider choices that shape scientific inquiry and interpretation.

topics.label: Science & evidence
topics.question: Which question about science matters most right now?

focuses.label: How can I judge a scientific claim?

steps.why: Start with the practices that make scientific claims open to scrutiny.
Separate causal evidence from a correlation or an anecdote.
Understand what expert agreement can and cannot tell you.
Look at reliability across studies rather than one striking result.
Use standards of inquiry to assess claims of scientific authority.
Bring the checks together for your own example.

focuses.label: How does science justify its conclusions?

steps.why: See the philosophical difficulty in learning general rules from past observations.
Examine testing by attempted refutation.
Ask what a failed prediction really tells us.
Compare scientific change with the picture of one test at a time.
Explore why an explanatory hypothesis can be reasonable without being certain.
Ask what successful science licenses us to believe about reality.

topics.label: News, experts & AI
topics.question: What makes this information hard to assess?

focuses.label: I need to decide which sources to trust

steps.why: Assess expertise when you cannot check every technical claim yourself.
Distinguish missing information from systems that undermine trust in outsiders.
Examine how information can mislead and how intent changes the problem.
Check whether you scrutinize unwelcome claims more than welcome ones.
Make an evidence check you can repeat on the next story.
Look beyond individual judgment to the institutions supporting reliable information.

focuses.label: I want to use AI without outsourcing my judgment

steps.why: Examine how assistance can support or weaken your own judgment.
Ask what justified reliance on another information source requires.
Check a generated answer against evidence you can inspect.
Separate an answer that sounds natural from one that is well supported.
Keep confidence proportionate when the source is opaque.

topics.label: Knowledge & skepticism
topics.question: Which philosophical problem draws you in?

focuses.label: What makes a belief count as knowledge?

steps.why: See why justified true belief may still fall short of knowledge.
Clarify what having reasons for a belief amounts to.
Explore whether chains of reasons need starting points.
Compare an alternative built around the relations among beliefs.
Test these accounts against a familiar source of knowledge.
Ask why knowledge matters beyond holding a true belief.

focuses.label: Can we know anything for certain?

steps.why: Distinguish different doubts before deciding how to answer them.
Reconstruct a central route from skeptical possibilities to doubt.
Compare ways of resisting the skeptical conclusion.
Ask whether knowledge can survive the possibility of error.
Keep the question of truth distinct from our certainty about it.
Examine whether disagreement makes truth relative.

topics.label: Identity, power & being heard
topics.question: Which question about identity and knowledge interests you?

focuses.label: Whose experiences and testimony are taken seriously?

steps.why: Examine harms people face specifically as knowers.
Explore how social position can shape access to evidence and inquiry.
Ask how situated perspectives can contribute to objective inquiry.
Examine how group commitments can affect the assessment of evidence.
Notice how descriptions shape what gets heard.
Consider changes to the conditions under which people contribute knowledge.

focuses.label: How do contested concepts shape a debate?

steps.why: Understand why some disagreements persist even after definitions are clarified.
Ask when changing a concept might improve inquiry.
Distinguish claims about social formation from claims about truth.
Connect conceptual disputes with perspectives and social positions.
Keep differences of perspective available for inquiry.

topics.label: Faith, values & responsible belief
topics.question: What is the main tension for you?

focuses.label: What do I owe the evidence when forming beliefs?

steps.why: Compare rival views of the responsibilities involved in believing.
Separate reasons a belief would be useful from reasons it is true.
Explore faith as a test case for evidence and justified belief.
Examine the view that justification should answer to evidence.
Hold a view with confidence that acknowledges its limits.
Decide what openness asks of you when disagreement remains.

focuses.label: How do facts and values connect?

steps.why: Distinguish factual premises from the values needed for a normative conclusion.
Ask whether moral stakes can affect the standards for knowing.
Examine the roles values play in a practice built around evidence.
Use the distinction to understand a concrete dispute.
Consider whether believing itself carries ethical obligations.

topics.label: Thinking habits & confidence
topics.question: What would you most like to improve?

focuses.label: Notice bias and change my mind more fairly

steps.why: Notice when you apply unequal standards to evidence.
Examine how desired conclusions can shape reasoning.
Compare practices intended to reduce reasoning errors.
Treat beliefs as maps you can revise rather than positions to defend.
Connect useful practices with longer-term intellectual habits.
Turn a reading session into a repeatable routine.

focuses.label: Match my confidence to what I know

steps.why: Check whether familiarity has been mistaken for understanding.
Compare confidence with outcomes rather than with a feeling of certainty.
Balance appropriate confidence with recognition of limits.
Practice judgments that can be checked later.
Make a conclusion with uncertainty stated rather than hidden.

topics.label: History & a broad introduction
topics.question: How would you like to enter the field?

steps.why: Get an overview of what epistemology asks before choosing a theory.
Build the vocabulary shared by the chapters that follow.
See recurring problems across different periods and traditions.
Learn a distinction used throughout philosophical arguments.
Meet a compact problem that reshaped the theory of knowledge.
Choose what you want to study next in the wider field.
Explore early debates about knowledge, perception and inquiry.
Compare another tradition’s investigations of sources of knowledge.
Examine debates connecting reason, experience and intellectual traditions.
Broaden the comparison through debates about names and knowing.
See how later skeptical and scientific questions transformed inquiry.
Follow historical questions into current research.
